{'': "Suspicious bulk orders of old books have led many booksellers to suspect that these books are being purchased on behalf of AI companies, to be scanned and used as training material without the authors' consent or payment."}

{'': 'A rare book among a bulk order was found to contain an AirTag, which was eventually sent to an Amazon AI training facility, seemingly confirming this theory.'}

{'': 'Booksellers specialising in second-hand books typically only receive orders for single copies or small batches of related titles. However, many of them have long reported receiving large orders for old books that appear to have no connection to one another.'}

{'': 'The suspicion is that these books are being purchased by AI companies, which then have their spines removed and the text fed into AI systems via high-speed scanning equipment, to be used as training material.'}

{'': "Not only is this done without the authors' consent, but no compensation is paid for the use of their work — at the very least, it is unethical, yet no concrete evidence has so far emerged to prove that this is happening. An investigation by 404 Media appears to have changed that."}

{'': 'The report is behind a paywall, but TNW has cited the findings, noting that the tracking device used was an AirTag, and that employees at the facility have confirmed the work being carried out there.'}

{'': "Older books are particularly valuable because any book published after 2022 may contain text written or edited by an AI system; in other words, this training data could be teaching AI systems to learn from other AIs' output. Although publishing contracts almost universally explicitly forbid authors from using AI-generated content, some are believed to be ignoring this restriction. As for self-published books, there are currently no effective regulatory measures in place."}

{'': 'Part of the problem is that intellectual property law has yet to catch up with such practices. While this would very likely be illegal in the UK, a 2025 ruling in the United States found it to be lawful, on the grounds that it constituted a transformative use of the copyrighted work.'}
